set.descent_text: The couloir exits at or near the notch on the West Ridge, with a little more low fifth-class ridge to the summit. From the top, the usual way down is south by the Cascadian Couloir: cross the Class 2-3 ground between the true and false summits (steep, often corniced snow early in the season), drop into the couloir and follow it down loose scree and talus to Ingalls Creek, then regain Longs Pass and walk out to the Esmeralda trailhead. Parties camped in the basin below the north side often prefer the Sherpa Glacier instead, which is the better early-season way back to camp. Carry an ice axe for the Cascadian, and keep clear of other parties, because the couloir sheds rock.

review.notes: Mount Stuart page: couloir tops out at the West Ridge notch, low class 5 to summit; Cascadian is the standard descent; Sherpa is the best early-season return to the basin camp. Trip report: icy couloir forced rappels on the way down. Longs Pass/Ingalls Creek detail from the existing row and sibling Cascadian text.

set.descent_text: Early in the season the Sherpa Glacier itself is the best way down: reverse the roughly 40-degree snow of the couloir, facing in, back to the camp in the basin at its foot. When the snow is hard and icy this becomes a no-fall descent that may need rappels to reach the glacier safely, so carry pickets or other anchors and rope. Later in the summer, or if you are leaving the basin for the south side, continue over the summit and down the Cascadian Couloir to Ingalls Creek and Longs Pass; that way is loose scree and talus and sheds rock onto anyone below.

review.notes: Mount Stuart page: Sherpa is the best early-season descent back to the basin camp, about 40 degrees; Cascadian is the standard descent. Trip report: hardpack crust required rappels on the way down.

set.descent_text: The route tops out very close to the true summit, so the way down is the Cascadian Couloir to the south. Cross the Class 2-3 ground between the true and false summits (steep, often corniced snow early in the season), then drop into the couloir and follow it down loose scree and talus to Ingalls Creek. The headwall base lies up-basin along the same drainage, so collect anything left there, then climb back to Longs Pass and walk out to the Esmeralda trailhead. Carry an ice axe through at least midsummer, and stay out from under other parties, as the couloir is notoriously loose.

review.notes: Mount Stuart page: Cascadian is the standard descent, class 2-3 between false and true summits, corniced snow early. Ingalls Creek/Longs Pass layout from the existing row and sibling approach text; the existing row says the route tops out near the true summit.

set.descent_text: Descend the West Ridge rather than reversing the East Ridge. From the summit, retrace the Class 3-4 ground and scramble ridge down to the low notch between Terror and The Rake, then go down the gully on the far side into Crescent Creek Basin. The gully is deep, narrow and loose, so expect rockfall and, in early season, snow or ice; it is descended with several rappels, including off a large chockstone, and downclimbing between them. The lower ridge has established anchors about 25 m apart, which suit short rappels or a belayed downclimb. Once in the basin, walk back to the Crescent Creek camp.

review.notes: Mount Terror page (archived): West Ridge/standard route goes through the loose, narrow gully to the Terror-Rake notch with established anchors about 25 m apart. Chockstone rappels and the summary of the West Ridge as the descent come from the existing row text.

set.descent_text: The route finishes on the summit ridge of Mount Washington, and the way down is the standard route rather than the SE Ridge, which would mean many rappels and the fifth-class cracks in reverse. Descend the Class 3-4 scramble to the basin; lingering snow often covers the upper slopes in early summer, and the narrow hourglass constriction can be bypassed on its west side. Below the basin, continue down through forest on the climbers' path to the FR-2419 trailhead at Big Creek, the same road end used for the approach.

review.notes: Route page: descend the Standard Route. Shield Wall trip report: about 90 min down Route 1. Standard-route trip report: basin snow, hourglass bypassed to the west on descent. Trailhead from the existing row.

set.approach: From the Mowich Lake trailhead, take the Spray Park Trail (the Wonderland Trail at first) about 3.5 miles to Spray Park at roughly 5,800 ft. Near 6,200 ft a way trail leaves the main trail, easy to follow for about a mile, and climbs toward the saddle between Echo Rock and Observation Rock near 7,600 ft. Stay on snow where you can to spare the meadows. The north side of Observation is steep and loose, so contour clockwise round the foot of the peak, crossing the east icefield of the Flett Glacier if it is in, to the scree and talus of the south slope, where the climb starts.
set.descent_text: Reverse the route: down the loose pumice of the south slope to the Echo-Observation saddle, then back along the way trail to Spray Park and the Spray Park Trail to Mowich Lake. Descend south and east only. Dropping west puts you on the crevassed Flett Glacier, which may be impassable late in the season. By August the snow slopes east of the summit can be icy, so carry an ice axe and crampons or microspikes, or circle well above or below them. Wear a helmet, since the rock is crumbly and anything knocked loose falls on those below.

review.notes: WTA: Mowich Lake, Spray Park, Flett Glacier traverse left to south side, scree to summit. Mountaineers Echo page: way trail at ~6,200 ft, saddle, clockwise contour, icy slopes east in August. Mountaineers N Face page: descend south and east, not west onto the Flett. Summit page: ~3.5 mi to Spray Park, east icefield to saddle, loose pumice.

set.descent_text: Reverse the line of ascent: the short rock scramble and the Class 2-3 snow couloir back down to the LeConte Glacier, then cross the glacier to the Le Conte-Sentinel col camp. In a high-snow year a couple of very short rappels off nuts or slings may be needed on the way down, so bring a few small pieces and cord. Watch the moat and bergschrund at the foot of the couloir, and rope up for the crevassed glacier on the return to camp.

review.notes: Old Guard page: west side is a class 2/3 snow couloir and short rock scramble from the LeConte Glacier; a climber's log reports two very short rappels off nuts and slings on the way down in a high-snow year. Camp location from the existing row; crevasse/moat caution is general to the glacier and thinly sourced.
